payload.explanation_text:
A cell membrane surrounds a cell. It controls what moves in and out.

Membrane phospholipids are amphipathic. This means they have two parts that relate to water in different ways. The head is hydrophilic, which means water-loving. The fatty acid tails are hydrophobic, which means water-avoiding.

In water, phospholipids form a double layer called a bilayer. The heads face the water on both sides. The tails are inside. Each layer of the bilayer is called a leaflet.

Fatty acids are carbon chains. Saturated chains have no carbon–carbon double bonds. They pack closely together. Unsaturated chains have double bonds. These bends stop tight packing. So unsaturated tails increase fluidity. Fluidity means how freely membrane parts move.

Several things affect fluidity. These include saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol.

Cholesterol acts as a buffer. It restrains excessive movement. It also helps prevent stiffening when the membrane is cold.

The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane. It is a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins. These components can move sideways.

The two leaflets are not identical. Lipids rarely switch leaflets on their own. Flippases, floppases, and scramblases help this movement.

Sugar chains on the outer surface form the glycocalyx, or sugar coating. It helps cells recognize each other. It also helps cells tell self from non-self.

concepts.name: Amphipathic phospholipids form the bilayer
concepts.taught_summary: Phospholipids have a water-loving head and water-avoiding tails. In water, the heads face outward and the tails face inward, forming a bilayer with two leaflets.

concepts.name: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids
concepts.taught_summary: Saturated tails have no double bonds and pack closely. Double bonds in unsaturated tails create bends that hinder packing and increase fluidity.

concepts.name: What affects membrane fluidity
concepts.taught_summary: Fluidity depends on fatty acid saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol.

concepts.name: Cholesterol as a fluidity buffer
concepts.taught_summary: Cholesterol restrains excessive movement when the membrane is very fluid and helps prevent stiffening when it is cold.

concepts.name: Fluid mosaic model
concepts.taught_summary: The membrane is a mosaic of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins, with components that can move sideways.

concepts.name: Membrane asymmetry and lipid flipping
concepts.taught_summary: The two leaflets differ in composition. Lipids rarely flip between leaflets without help from flippases, floppases, and scramblases.

concepts.name: Glycocalyx and cell recognition
concepts.taught_summary: Sugar chains on the outer surface form the glycocalyx, which helps cells recognize each other and distinguish self from non-self.
